newsitem.title: USA: Progress looks slow at last-ditch EU, U.S. meat talks.
newsitem.headline: Progress looks slow at last-ditch EU, U.S. meat talks.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials met into Tuesday night to settle an escalating dispute over meat imports, but sources said Wednesday it did not appear that much progress had been made.
The officials, who started their talks Tuesday afternoon, met for more than seven hours into the evening, then resumed negotiations early Wednesday afternoon.
Washington and Brussels are trying to resolve a nasty fight that threatens to disrupt the trans-Atlantic trade of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of meat and poultry.

The negotiators remain stuck on a handful of key points, said sources close to the talks. An agreement over eggs and dairy shipments appears close at hand, but on some critical poultry and meat issues, sources did not report any movement.
"Not a whole lot happened ... I'm just not that optimistic," said a U.S. industry official who had been briefed on the Tuesday session.
European officials agreed there were still problems.
"We're still very much at it," said EU spokeswoman Ella Krucoff. "A few things have gone well, but there are still some important outstanding issues to resolve."
Krucoff said the EU negotiating team was scheduled to return to Brussels Thursday afternoon, but added that if progress was being made, officials would remain in Washington for more talks.

The negotiators have been trying to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks which ended last week without agreement by an April 1 deadline. An agreement would allow each side to import meat and poultry from the other even if inspection methods differ.
The unsuccessful conclusion of last week's talks prompted moves on both sides of the Atlantic to restrict trade.

The European Union on April 1 adopted new poultry import inspection standards that immediately halted U.S. poultry shipments to the EU, and could mean the loss of up to $100 million worth of poultry and dairy sales.
In response to the new EU rules, the United States implemented new regulations that require EU meat and poultry plants to comply with U.S. inspection standards by April 15.
The new U.S. regulations could halt some $300 million worth of imports of European meat products, mostly Danish pork products and Italian hams.
Negotiators are now trying to reach an agreement before April 15 when Washington has said it will remove more than 100 EU plants from its list of approved exporters.

One of the key issues left to be resolved is the process used by the U.S. poultry and meat industry to decontaminate products. This has been a major sticking point especially with American poultry processors.
Also being fought over is the use of wooden pallets, platforms used to move boxes of meat and poultry, favoured by U.S. packers. The Europeans are insisting on plastic pallets.

Finally, the U.S. meat industry is concerned over the role of EU inspectors in the U.S. plant inspection approval process, and says EU inspectors should only be involved in reviews and auditing, as U.S. inspectors are in Europe.
